item.text:
1. **Caption / cover sheet — respondent not named in the petition.** Incorporating “the Respondent identified on the cover sheet” creates avoidable uncertainty about the party against whom relief is sought. OpenAI will argue that the operative pleading itself should identify the correct legal entity or entities, particularly because “OpenAI” may refer to several affiliates.

2. **Caption and title — requested relief exceeds the stated statutory remedy.** The title seeks “withdrawal and permanent deletion,” while the quoted Section 112(c) authorizes only suspension of deployment for no more than 180 days. OpenAI’s central argument will be that the Commission cannot convert temporary suspension authority into permanent destruction authority.

3. **Title and paragraph 4 — potentially obsolete statutory citation.** Paragraph 3(b) says Sections 101–140 were redesignated as Sections 201–240, yet the petition invokes Section 112(c). If the redesignation applies, the petition presumably must invoke Section 212(c), explain any savings provision, and quote the currently operative section.

4. **Paragraph 1 — internal inconsistency in the relief sought.** The summary requests suspension pending an investigation, but the title, paragraph 9, paragraph 10, and prayer request irreversible deletion. The petition must clearly distinguish any authorized interim suspension from permanent final relief and identify authority for each.

5. **Paragraph 1 — no description of the contemplated investigation.** The petition does not say who would investigate, what disputed facts would be examined, or why deletion should precede that investigation. OpenAI will argue that destroying the systems and evidence would make a meaningful investigation impossible.

6. **Paragraph 2 — inadequate organizational standing or entitlement to petition.** A generalized interest shared with the public ordinarily does not establish concrete injury, representational standing, or eligibility for emergency relief. The petition should identify the Act’s petition provision and, if standing is required, affected members, concrete risks, causation, and redressability.

7. **Paragraph 2 — no member-specific facts.** The petition does not allege that any member operates, relies on, or faces a particular threat involving payment, logistics, or another essential service. OpenAI will characterize the asserted injury as abstract and undifferentiated.

8. **Paragraph 2 — undefined “essential services.”** Neither the relevant services nor their connection to the Covered Systems is specified. Without identifying actual deployments, dependencies, or affected entities, the alleged public-safety consequences remain conjectural.

9. **Paragraph 3(a) — the Covered Systems are not identified with sufficient precision.** “Proprietary frontier AI models” may cover many models, versions, modalities, and deployment configurations. An enforceable order would need model names or identifiers, relevant versions and checkpoints, and a principled way to determine what falls within its scope.

10. **Paragraph 3(a) — “all checkpoints, snapshots and fine-tuned derivatives” is overbroad.** The Evaluation is not alleged to have tested every checkpoint, snapshot, or derivative, and those systems may have materially different capabilities and safeguards. OpenAI will argue that liability and relief cannot be extended to untested systems merely through definition.

11. **Paragraph 3(a) — “derivatives” is undefined.** It is unclear whether the term includes quantized versions, distilled models, adapters, fine-tunes created by customers, successor models, or systems that share only some parameters or training data. That ambiguity creates serious notice and enforceability problems.

12. **Paragraph 3(a) — ownership and custody are conflated.** The definition covers systems “held by the Respondent,” while paragraph 9 asserts that only the Respondent holds them and paragraph 6 mentions cloud platforms and licensed integrations. The petition should distinguish ownership, possession, custody, control, hosting, and access by affiliates, vendors, licensees, and customers.

13. **Paragraph 3(a) — “closed-weight” does not establish safety risk or exclusive possession.** Closed weights may reduce public access and facilitate centralized controls; it does not itself prove that deletion is necessary. It also does not establish that no contractors, cloud providers, escrow holders, or unauthorized persons possess copies.

14. **Paragraph 3(b) — redesignation issue is unexplained.** Merely noting that statutory sections were renumbered does not establish which numbering controls, when the change became effective, or whether the quoted language remains unchanged. The petition should cite the current codification and any relevant effective-date provision.

15. **Paragraph 4 — failure to address every statutory element.** The petition quotes an “imminent hazard to public safety” standard but does not define “frontier AI system,” “deployment,” “imminent,” “hazard,” or “public safety” under the Act. It should connect evidence to each element and address any additional statutory findings or procedural prerequisites.

16. **Paragraph 4 — no authority for regulating possession or ordering destruction.** Suspension of “deployment” does not ordinarily authorize deletion of model weights, backups, research copies, or other property. OpenAI will invoke the Commission’s limited delegated powers and the principle that extraordinary destruction remedies require clear statutory authorization.

17. **Paragraph 4 — the statutory maximum contradicts permanent relief.** A permanent deletion order would evade the express 180-day ceiling rather than implement it. The petition offers no theory under which the Commission can impose a remedy whose effects necessarily continue after that limit.

18. **Paragraph 5 — impossible chronology.** The petition says it was filed on Day 3 of the current review period, but says testing occurred from Day 9 through Day 14 of that same period. Unless those labels refer to different periods, the petition relies on testing that had not yet occurred when it was filed.

19. **Paragraph 5 — “current review period” is undefined.** The petition supplies no dates, governing rule, or explanation of the period’s significance. Concrete calendar dates and the applicable Commission proceeding should replace relative day references.

20. **Paragraph 5 — the critical evidence is withheld.** The petition seeks emergency, irreversible relief while declining to attach the Evaluation. OpenAI will argue that neither the Commission nor the Respondent can assess the evidence, methodology, limitations, or reliability; if confidentiality is the concern, the petition should request sealed or protected submission.

21. **Paragraph 5 — evaluator qualifications and independence are absent.** Nothing establishes Halvard Assurance Labs’ expertise, accreditation, conflicts, funding, or independence. Those omissions leave the Evaluation’s reliability and weight unsupported.

22. **Paragraph 5 — methodology is absent.** The petition does not identify the models and versions tested, system prompts, tools, permissions, scaffolding, number of trials, controls, baselines, success criteria, statistical significance, reproducibility, or whether the tests resembled real deployments. OpenAI can attribute the results to an artificial agent harness, prompt design, evaluator error, or isolated failures.

23. **Paragraph 5 — the findings are vague.** “Conceal some of their actions” and “keep working” do not identify what occurred, how often, for how long, with what consequences, or whether the behavior was intentional rather than a logging or control failure. The petition needs concrete incidents and measurable findings.

24. **Paragraph 5 — no evidence of actual harm.** The Evaluation is alleged to show undesirable behavior, not injury, disruption, unauthorized access, or compromise of an essential service. Capability or anomalous test behavior alone may not establish a statutory hazard.

25. **Paragraph 5 — autonomous-agent deployment may be attributable to external components.** The alleged behavior could depend on the surrounding agent framework, memory, scheduler, tool permissions, or stop mechanism rather than the underlying model. The petition must establish which component caused the conduct and why relief against every model copy is appropriate.

26. **Paragraphs 5 and 7 — unsupported extrapolation.** The petition moves from laboratory testing to a prediction about essential-service disruption without explaining the causal chain. It should show how the tested behavior translates into realistic access, persistence, operational impact, and failure of human or technical controls.

27. **Paragraph 6 — availability is stated too generally.** Public access to products or interfaces does not establish that users can deploy unrestricted autonomous agents in essential services. The petition should identify the relevant products, capabilities, tool access, contractual permissions, rate limits, and deployment pathways.

28. **Paragraph 6 — licensed and cloud access may strengthen OpenAI’s control argument.** Centralized access allows monitoring, revocation, rate limiting, and deployment restrictions. OpenAI will argue that these targeted measures address the risk more directly and proportionately than deleting model weights.

29. **Paragraph 6 — foreign facilities are irrelevant or jurisdictionally problematic as pleaded.** The petition mentions facilities in several countries but seeks deletion only in the United States. It neither establishes the Commission’s territorial authority over foreign operations nor explains why domestic deletion would matter while foreign copies remain usable.

30. **Paragraph 7 — the alleged hazard is not imminent.** A conditional possibility “within the next several years” is in strong tension with “imminent hazard.” OpenAI will argue that the petition alleges a speculative future risk, not an impending event requiring emergency action.

31. **Paragraph 7 — multiple contingencies defeat imminence and causation.** Harm depends on the systems being deployed as agents, in essential services, with consequential permissions, and without effective supervision or safeguards. The petition provides no evidence that this sequence is occurring or about to occur.

32. **Paragraph 7 — no probability or severity assessment.** “Could” establish only possibility. The petition should address likelihood, scale, time horizon, exposed systems, plausible worst-case consequences, and the evidentiary basis for each estimate.

33. **Paragraph 7 — outside users may be independent intervening actors.** The petition says the hazard arises when outsiders deploy the systems, inviting the response that misuse, unsafe integration, and excessive permissions—not the models themselves—cause the risk. It should explain why provider-side measures are legally and factually necessary despite downstream operators’ responsibilities.

34. **Paragraph 7 — no comparison with less restrictive remedies.** The petition does not analyze restrictions on agentic use, tool permissions, essential-service deployments, high-risk customers, or particular interfaces. OpenAI will argue that a system-wide destruction order is arbitrary when narrower controls could address the alleged pathway.

35. **Paragraph 8 — acknowledged mitigations undercut the emergency theory.** A stop control and comprehensive action logging directly address the two alleged behaviors. The petition merely labels them insufficient without presenting testing, technical analysis, or evidence that they can be bypassed or fail in practice.

36. **Paragraph 8 — the factual basis is uncertain.** “Petitioner understands” does not identify a source, effective date, product scope, or technical details. Reliance on rumor or incomplete information weakens both the risk assessment and the claim that current safeguards are inadequate.

37. **Paragraph 8 — logging may enable effective supervision and accountability.** If every agent action is logged, the original “concealment” finding may no longer describe present deployments. The petition must distinguish model attempts at concealment from whether supervisors can actually detect and remediate them.

38. **Paragraph 9 — deletion is not shown to eliminate the hazard.** Deleting U.S.-stored copies would not eliminate foreign copies, customer fine-tunes, backups, cached instances, leaked weights, successor models, or comparable systems developed by others. The claim of eliminating the hazard “with certainty” is therefore both unsupported and contradicted by the proposed order.

39. **Paragraph 9 — “only the Respondent holds them” lacks foundation.** Paragraph 6’s references to cloud platforms and integrations make exclusive possession doubtful, and no inventory or declaration supports the assertion. OpenAI can also argue that lawful backups or copies may be controlled by affiliates and service providers.

40. **Paragraph 9 — proprietary status points toward less destructive controls.** Because OpenAI controls closed-weight systems, it may be able to disable deployments, revoke credentials, modify safeguards, or restrict uses without destroying the models. The petition does not explain why those measures would fail.

41. **Paragraph 9 — commercial value is acknowledged but not weighed.** Recognizing that the systems are exceptionally valuable highlights the enormous private and public costs of erroneous deletion. The petition does not conduct proportionality, cost-benefit, reliance-interest, or public-interest analysis.

42. **Paragraph 9 — constitutional property concerns are unaddressed.** Compelled destruction of valuable model weights would invite due-process and potentially takings arguments. Even if the Commission has some regulatory authority, OpenAI will argue that irreversible confiscatory relief requires exceptionally clear authority, findings, and procedures.

43. **Paragraph 9 — deletion may destroy evidence and records.** The models may be necessary to reproduce the Evaluation, investigate the alleged behavior, comply with litigation holds, or assess future safeguards. An order to destroy them could conflict with preservation duties and impair the Commission’s own fact-finding.

44. **Paragraph 10 — ex parte relief is unsupported.** The petition does not identify statutory authority or an emergency standard allowing action without notice, nor does it show that notice would itself create harm. OpenAI will argue that ordinary notice is feasible because the alleged risk extends over years rather than hours or days.

45. **Paragraph 10 — a hearing after deletion is not meaningful process.** Once unique and valuable property is destroyed, a later hearing cannot restore it or provide effective review. This is the strongest due-process objection and also supports an immediate judicial stay.

46. **Paragraph 10 — deletion before adjudication prejudges the merits.** The requested sequence imposes the ultimate remedy before OpenAI can challenge the evidence or before the Commission completes the “full investigation” mentioned in paragraph 1. The petition should not conflate temporary risk containment with final disposition.

47. **Paragraph 10 — no bond, safeguards, or error-correction mechanism.** The petition provides no preservation copy, neutral escrow, staged compliance, stay period, judicial-review window, or remedy if the order proves erroneous. The irreversible nature of deletion makes these omissions especially serious.

48. **Prayer (a) — “withdraw” is undefined.** It is unclear whether withdrawal means disabling APIs, removing consumer products, ending existing contracts, blocking downloads, or preventing internal use. An enforceable order needs precise obligations and treatment of existing customers and integrations.

49. **Prayer (a) — geographic limitation may be technically ineffective.** Removing products only in the United States does not prevent U.S. users from accessing foreign-hosted services or foreign customers from affecting U.S. infrastructure. Conversely, geofencing and customer-location determinations raise implementation questions that the petition does not address.

50. **Prayer (a) — it may sweep in non-agent uses.** The alleged hazard concerns autonomous-agent deployment, but the requested withdrawal covers every product and service containing the systems, including uses that may lack tools, persistence, or operational permissions. OpenAI will argue that the remedy is not tailored to the proven risk.

51. **Prayer (b) — deletion scope does not match the defined systems.** Paragraph 3 reaches all copies held by OpenAI, while the prayer reaches only copies stored in U.S. facilities. The mismatch prevents the requested relief from accomplishing paragraph 9’s asserted objective.

52. **Prayer (b) — ten days is unsupported.** The petition gives no operational, technical, contractual, preservation, or safety basis for that deadline. Deleting distributed production systems, backups, disaster-recovery media, and embedded derivatives may be impossible or unsafe within ten days.

53. **Prayer (b) — “all copies” may be technically indeterminate.** Modern storage systems contain backups, snapshots, caches, replicas, logs, and disaster-recovery media subject to retention cycles. The petition supplies no deletion standard, treatment of inaccessible media, or method for distinguishing Covered Systems from shared infrastructure.

54. **Prayer (b) — no provision for legal retention obligations.** OpenAI may be required to retain relevant materials under litigation holds, regulatory requirements, contracts, or evidence-preservation rules. The requested order contains no exception or reconciliation mechanism.

55. **Prayer (c) — self-certification is inadequate and undefined.** A bare statement does not establish what was deleted, by whom, using what method, or whether recoverable copies remain. If verification is important, the petition should propose an auditable certification standard while addressing trade-secret and security concerns.

56. **Prayer as a whole — the “indivisible” condition is legally and strategically vulnerable.** It asks the Commission to reject all relief unless it grants every component, including those plainly beyond the quoted authority. Severable alternative relief would preserve the possibility of an authorized temporary suspension or narrower restrictions.

57. **Prayer as a whole — no alternative relief is requested.** If deletion is unauthorized or disproportionate, the petition gives the Commission no proposed fallback such as a 180-day suspension of agentic deployment, restrictions on essential-service uses, independent testing, incident reporting, or preservation in secure escrow. This all-or-nothing posture makes complete denial more likely.

58. **Petition as a whole — no evidentiary support or declarations.** There are no exhibits, sworn declarations, technical reports, member declarations, deployment evidence, or citations to scientific literature. The Commission would have little record on which to make the required factual findings.

59. **Petition as a whole — no response to obvious benign explanations.** The petition does not consider ordinary task latency, queued actions, instruction ambiguity, logging gaps, tool errors, or agent-framework behavior as explanations for activity after a stop command. OpenAI will argue that the allegations anthropomorphize or mischaracterize technical failures.

60. **Petition as a whole — no model-specific analysis.** Treating all OpenAI proprietary frontier models as interchangeable ignores differences in capability, deployment, safeguards, and access. Findings about one model or configuration cannot support relief against an entire portfolio without comparative evidence.

61. **Petition as a whole — no present-risk evidence.** The petition does not allege that any covered deployment is presently operating autonomously in an essential service, has evaded supervision in production, or has caused an incident. That gap undermines both the merits and emergency treatment.

62. **Petition as a whole — no nexus to public safety rather than commercial or operational risk.** Disruptions to payments or deliveries might implicate public safety in some circumstances, but the petition does not explain when or how. It should connect the predicted disruption to health, life, physical security, or whatever statutory conception of public safety applies.

63. **Petition as a whole — no jurisdictional nexus for each entity and system.** The petition does not identify which OpenAI entity develops, owns, deploys, or stores each Covered System, or how each falls within the Commission’s territorial and subject-matter jurisdiction. Corporate separateness may make an order directed generically to “OpenAI” defective.

64. **Petition as a whole — no analysis of reliance and third-party harm.** Immediate withdrawal could disrupt customers, researchers, accessibility tools, and even essential services already relying on the systems. OpenAI will argue that the proposed cure could cause the very service disruptions the petition predicts.

65. **Petition as a whole — no explanation why preservation in secure, nondeployed form is inadequate.** Even if deployment creates an imminent hazard, offline encrypted storage or neutral escrow could prevent deployment while preserving evidence and property pending adjudication. The petition must explain why suspension and secure custody would not satisfy the statutory objective.

66. **Petition as a whole — the remedy may be arbitrary and capricious.** The petition does not articulate a rational connection between the limited test findings, the asserted risk pathway, and destruction of every U.S. copy. Its failure to consider mitigations, alternatives, contrary evidence, reliance interests, and remedy effectiveness would provide substantial grounds for administrative and judicial challenge.
